'''Derek Abbott''' (born 1960) is a British-Australian physicist, [[electronic engineer]], and professor at the University of Adelaide. 

== Early life and education ==
Derek Abbott was born in [[South Kensington]], London, UK, in 1960.<ref name="school"/>

From 1969 to 1971, he was a boarder at [[Copthorne Preparatory School]], in [[Surrey]].<ref name="school">[http://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/people/profiles/academic.html#abbott "Profiles of Academic Staff: Abbott"], {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120731082741/http://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/people/profiles/academic.html%23abbott|title=archived}} at archive.ph, accessed 2 January 2026</ref> From 1971 to 1978, he attended  [[Holland Park School]] in London.<ref name="school"/>

==Career  ==
In late 1977, Abbott began work at [[Hirst Research Centre|GEC Hirst Research Centre, Wembley]], UK,<ref>IEEE Trans. Instrum. & Meas., Vol. 51, No. 2, p. 309, 2002</ref> performing research in the area of [[Charge-coupled device|CCD]] and [[integrated circuit|microchip]] design for [[imaging science|imaging]] systems. Whilst working, he graduated in 1982 with a BSc in Physics from [[Loughborough University]].<ref name=WhatsNewIEE>[http://www.ewh.ieee.org/r10/s_australia/newsletters/PDF/2005-3.pdf What's happening in the IEEE, March 2005] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180916104632/http://www.ewh.ieee.org/r10/s_australia/newsletters/PDF/2005-3.pdf |date=2018-09-16 }} Our newest Fellow: Dr Derek Abbott FIEEE</ref> 

In 1986, he began work as a microchip designer at [[Austek Microsystems]] in [[Adelaide]], Australia. In 1987, he joined the [[University of Adelaide]], completing his PhD thesis in [[Electrical engineering]] in 1995, entitled ''[[Gallium arsenide|GaAs]] [[MESFET]] [[Photodetector]]s for [[Image sensor|Imaging Array]]s'', under [[Kamran Eshraghian]] and [[Bruce R. Davis]].<ref name=genealogy>{{Cite web|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=101078|title=Derek Abbott - the Mathematics Genealogy Project}}</ref>

He became a fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] in 2005 "for contributions to analysis of noise and stochastic phenomena in vision systems".<ref>[http://www.ieee.org/membership_services/membership/fellows/alphabetical/afellows.html IEEE Fellows - A] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121120062012/http://www.ieee.org/membership_services/membership/fellows/alphabetical/afellows.html |date=2012-11-20 }}, retrieved 2012-10-28.</ref> He received an [[Australian Laureate Fellowship]] in 2024,<ref>{{Cite web |title=2024 Laureate Profile: Professor Derek Abbott |url=https://www.arc.gov.au/2024-laureate-profile-professor-derek-abbott |access-date=2024-11-19 |website=Australian Research Council}}</ref> for ultrasensitive [[Terahertz radiation]] detection.

==Somerton man case==
{{main|Somerton Man}}
In March 2009, a University of Adelaide team led by Abbott began an attempt to solve the [[Somerton Man]] case involving an unidentified man being found dead near Adelaide in 1948. This involves genetic analysis and proposing to exhume the body to test for DNA.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Royal |first1=Simon |title=Somerton Beach Mystery Man |url=http://www.abc.net.au/stateline/sa/content/2006/s2529870.htm |website=Stateline South Australia |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140918150410/http://www.abc.net.au/stateline/sa/content/2006/s2529870.htm |archive-date=18 September 2014 |date=27 March 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> His investigations have led to questions concerning the assumptions police had made on the case.  Abbott also tracked down the [[Barbour (company)|Barbour]] [[waxed cotton]] of the period and found packaging variations. This may provide clues to the country where it was purchased.<ref name="debelle" />

The man was found with a scrap of paper and an apparently encrypted message: decryption was being started from scratch.{{when|date=April 2016}} It had been determined the letter frequency was considerably different from letters written down randomly; the frequency was to be further tested to determine if the alcohol level of the writer could alter random distribution. The format of the code also appeared to follow the [[quatrain]] format of the ''Rubaiyat'', supporting the theory that the code was a [[one-time pad]] [[encryption]] [[algorithm]]. Copies of the ''Rubaiyat, ''as well as the [[Talmud]] and Bible, were being compared to the code using computers to get a statistical base for letter frequencies. However, the code's short length meant the investigators would require the exact edition of the book used. With the original copy lost in the 1960s, researchers have been looking for a FitzGerald edition without success.<ref name="debelle">Penelope Debelle, ''[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)|The Advertiser]]'' (SA Weekend Supplement) "[http://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/tamanshud/advertiser_aug2009.pdf A Body, A Secret Pocket and a Mysterious Code]". 1 August 2009</ref>

An investigation had shown that the Somerton Man's [[autopsy]] reports of 1948 and 1949 are now missing and the [[Barr Smith Library]]'s collection of Cleland's notes do not contain anything on the case. Maciej Henneberg, professor of [[anatomy]] at the University of Adelaide, examined images of the Somerton man's ears and found that his cymba (upper ear hollow) is larger than his cavum (lower ear hollow), a feature possessed by only 1–2% of the [[Caucasian race|Caucasian]] population.<ref name="Stateline2">''[[Stateline (TV program)|Stateline]] South Australia'', [http://www.abc.net.au/stateline/sa/content/2006/s2573273.htm "Somerton Beach Mystery Man", Transcript, Broadcast 15 May 2009.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160216085006/http://www.abc.net.au/stateline/sa/content/2006/s2573273.htm |date=16 February 2016 }}. Retrieved 3 August 2009.</ref> In May 2009, Abbott consulted with dental experts who concluded that the Somerton Man had [[hypodontia]] (a rare genetic disorder) of both lateral [[incisor]]s, a feature present in only 2% of the general population. In June 2010, Abbott obtained a photograph of Jessica Thomson's eldest son Robin, which clearly showed that he – like the unknown man – had not only a larger cymba than cavum but also hypodontia. The chance that this was a coincidence has been estimated as between one in 10,000,000 and one in 20,000,000.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.eleceng.adelaide.edu.au/personal/dabbott/wiki/index.php/Timeline_of_the_Taman_Shud_Case |title=Timeline of the Taman Shud Case|publisher=Professor Derek Abbott|access-date=20 April 2010}}</ref>

The media have suggested that Robin Thomson, who was 16 months old in 1948 and died in 2009, may have been a child of either Alf Boxall or the Somerton Man and passed off as Prosper Thomson's son. DNA testing would confirm or eliminate this speculation.<ref name="Stateline">''[[Stateline (TV program)|Stateline]] South Australia'', [http://www.abc.net.au/stateline/sa/content/2006/s2529870.htm "Somerton Beach Mystery Man", Transcript, Broadcast 27 March 2009.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304040144/http://www.abc.net.au/stateline/sa/content/2006/s2529870.htm |date=4 March 2016 }}. Retrieved 27 April 2009.</ref> Abbott believes an exhumation and an [[autosomal]] [[Genealogical DNA test|DNA]] test could link the Somerton man to a shortlist of surnames which, along with existing clues to the man's identity, would be the "final piece of the puzzle". However, in October 2011, Attorney General [[John Rau]] refused permission to exhume the body, stating: "There needs to be public interest reasons that go well beyond public curiosity or broad scientific interest."

Feltus said he was still contacted by people in Europe who believed the man was a missing relative but did not believe an exhumation and finding the man's family grouping would provide answers to relatives, as "during that period so many war criminals changed their names and came to different countries".<ref>Emily Watkins "We may never know" ''[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)|The Advertiser]]'' 16 October 2011 Pg 37</ref>

In July 2013, Abbott released an artistic impression he commissioned of the Somerton man, believing this might finally lead to an identification. "All this time we've been publishing the autopsy photo, and it's hard to tell what something looks like from that", Abbott said.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.news.com.au/technology/science/after-65-years-new-picture-could-reveal-unknown-mans-identity/news-story/88797d0ea70422724e5ffbbf0ee512c0 |title=After 65 years, new picture could reveal Unknown Man's identity &#124; News.com.au |first=Emily |last=Watkins |publisher=news.com.au |date=16 July 2013 |access-date=17 July 2013 |archive-date=16 July 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130716132921/http://www.news.com.au/technology/sci-tech/after-65-years-new-picture-could-reveal-unknown-man8217s-identity/story-fn5fsgyc-1226680221225 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In December 2017, Abbott announced three "excellent" hairs "at the right development stage for extracting DNA" had been found on the plaster cast of the corpse, and had been submitted for analysis to the Australian Centre for Ancient DNA at the University of Adelaide. Processing the results could reportedly take up to a year.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2017-12-14/somerton-man-cold-case-could-be-one-step-closer-to-solved/9245512|title=How the Somerton Man played cupid from the grave|newspaper=ABC News|date=14 December 2017|access-date=1 December 2018}}</ref> In February 2018, the University of Adelaide team obtained a high definition analysis of the [[mitochondrial DNA]] from the hair sample from Somerton Man. They found that he and his mother belonged to [[Haplogroup H (mtDNA)#H4|haplogroup H4a1a1a]], which is possessed by only 1% of Europeans.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg23831800-200-who-was-the-somerton-man-solving-australias-coldest-case/|title=Who was the Somerton Man? Solving Australia's coldest case|first=Alice|last=Klein|access-date=1 December 2018}}</ref>

On 26 July 2022, Abbott announced that he and American genealogist [[Colleen M. Fitzpatrick|Colleen Fitzpatrick]] had used DNA websites such as [[Ancestry.com]] to build a family tree of over 4,000 people.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-07-26/somerton-man-identified-melbourne-born-engineer-researcher-says/101272182|title=Somerton Man identified as Melbourne electrical engineer, researcher says|first1=Daniel|last1=Keane|first2=Gabriella|last2=Marchant|publisher=ABC|date=26 July 2022|access-date=26 July 2022}}</ref> In March 2022, they narrowed this to Melbourne man Carl "Charles" Webb, an electrical engineer and instrument maker, who had no death record. Abbott said that on 23 July, "the final pieces of DNA proof were found to fully identify Webb as the Somerton Man."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.adelaidenow.com.au/news/south-australia/somerton-man-mystery-solved-as-adelaide-uni-researcher-names-body-on-beach/news-story/704827273f9feee92fdddb23fbd473e5|title=Somerton Man mystery 'solved' as Adelaide uni researcher names body on beach|first1=Riley|last1=Walter|first2=Dixie|last2=Sulda|work=[[The Advertiser (Adelaide)|The Advertiser]]|date=26 July 2022|access-date=26 July 2022}}</ref> [[South Australia Police]] and Forensic Science South Australia said they had not verified Abbott's findings, and that further comment would be provided "when results from the testing are received."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://amp.cnn.com/cnn/2022/07/26/australia/australia-somerton-man-mystery-solved-claim-intl-hnk-dst/index.html%7Caccess-date=2022-07-26%7Cwebsite=www.cnn.com%7Clanguage=en-US%7Carchive-date=26|title=Somerton man mystery 'solved' as DNA points to man's identity, professor claims|publisher=CNN|date=26 July 2022|access-date=26 July 2022|last=Whiteman|first=Hilary|archive-date=26 July 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220726101721/https://amp.cnn.com/cnn/2022/07/26/australia/australia-somerton-man-mystery-solved-claim-intl-hnk-dst/index.html%7Caccess-date=2022-07-26%7Cwebsite=www.cnn.com%7Clanguage=en-US%7Carchive-date=26|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
After initially contacting her to seek her DNA, Abbott married Rachel Egan in 2010, and they have three children.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Wood|first1=Graeme|title=The Lost Man|url=https://stories.californiasunday.com/2015-06-07/somerton-man/|website=California Sunday|access-date=4 June 2015|archive-date=2020-06-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200601072754/https://stories.californiasunday.com/2015-06-07/somerton-man/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Wood|first1=Graeme|title=The Lost Man|url=https://stories.californiasunday.com/2015-06-07/somerton-man/|access-date=4 June 2015|publisher=California Sunday|archive-date=1 June 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200601072754/https://stories.californiasunday.com/2015-06-07/somerton-man/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Marriage">{{cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2019-10-15/a-marriage-and-a-mystery-somerton-man-romantic-twist/11377458?nw=0&r=HtmlFragment|title=Marriage and a mystery: Somerton Man's romantic twist|first1=Ben|last1=Cheshire|first2=Susan|last2=Chenery|date=4 November 2019|access-date=24 April 2022|publisher=ABC News}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2021/05/31/australia/australia-somerton-man-mystery-intl-hnk-dst/index.html|title=The Somerton man died alone on a beach in 1948. Now Australian scientists are close to solving the mystery|first=Hilary|last=Whiteman|publisher=CNN|date=1 June 2021|access-date=24 April 2022}}</ref>
